title: What moved in Swiss markets while the policy rate stayed at zero
summary: Switzerland’s overnight rate was still close to zero in September, but its ten-year bond yield had risen, the franc had fallen and banks were still expanding their mortgage books. That combination is the starting point for reading the SNB’s third-quarter bulletin. Published on 30 September, the monetary policy report uses information available for the 24 September assessment. The accompanying survey records what 210 companies told the SNB between 21 July and 8 September. Together they show how financial prices, borrowing and corporate decisions evolved over different intervals around an unchanged policy rate. Most of the movements described were already under way before the September announcement (monetary policy report, pp. 4–7, 22–27; company interviews, pp. 28–34).

Overnight implementation worked much as the SNB intended. Secured overnight borrowing, measured by SARON, cost around –0.04% in mid-September. Sight deposits up to the applicable threshold earned 0% and balances above it earned –0.25%. On 1 August the SNB reduced the threshold factor for institutions subject to minimum reserves from 15 to 13.5. It auctioned one-week liquidity-absorbing repos daily and bills with maturities from one month to one year weekly. Average amounts outstanding since the June assessment were CHF 75.1 billion and CHF 78.8 billion, respectively. Average total sight deposits fell from CHF 468.5 billion in the week ending 12 June to CHF 454.0 billion in the week ending 11 September. The same balance sheet was being used to manage overnight liquidity, so that decline alone provides no estimate of currency intervention (pp. 22–23, chart 5.1).

Borrowing at longer maturities became more expensive. The ten-year Confederation yield rose from 0.39% in mid-June to 0.58% in mid-September. The yield curve shifted higher and flattened slightly because short and intermediate maturities rose more than yields beyond ten years. The SNB attributed most of that shift to higher expected short-term rates. Foreign yields also rose, generally by more. With short-term inflation expectations a little lower and longer-term expectations broadly stable, Swiss real rates increased. Households saw a different magnitude of change depending on the price observed. The published ten-year fixed mortgage rate had hovered around 2% since the beginning of 2026. The mortgage reference rate used to adjust existing rents was 1.25% in September. The reference rate and a currently quoted loan measure different stages of the transmission to housing costs (pp. 18–19, 23, 26, charts 5.2–5.3 and 5.11).

The franc moved in the opposite direction to real rates. It lost 2.8% on a trade-weighted nominal basis from mid-June to mid-September, including 2.2% against the euro and 3.8% against the dollar. With a 42% index weight, the euro mattered more for Swiss import prices and exporters’ overall currency exposure than its smaller bilateral move might suggest. Wider foreign–Swiss rate differentials made franc-funded carry trades more attractive, while the currency still appreciated briefly during episodes of uncertainty. The SNB offered an explanation for incentives, without measuring positions. Domestic equities also rewarded a closer look. The Swiss Market Index finished near its June level, but healthcare and financials in the broader Swiss Performance Index rose 4.4% and 2.1% respectively, while industrials and retail staples ended little changed. Treating the aggregate as the response of a representative Swiss company would miss that dispersion (pp. 24–25, charts 5.4–5.8).

Depositors adjusted their portfolios more visibly than borrowers adjusted loan balances. Between May and August, year-on-year growth in M1 slowed from 14.1% to 6.3%, in M2 from 9.6% to 4.0%, and in M3 from 4.5% to 3.5%. As capital-market yields rose relative to sight and savings rates, leaving money in liquid bank accounts became less attractive. Lending growth changed little. Mortgage claims grew 3.0% year on year in the second quarter and 3.1% in July, compared with 3.3% in the final quarter of 2025. Prices of owner-occupied apartments and apartment buildings rose faster in the second quarter than their ten-year average pace. These data offer distinct tests of transmission through deposit allocation, new financing costs and credit outstanding. The report also identifies classification adjustments to its lending series that matter when comparing this vintage with data downloaded subsequently (pp. 25–27, charts 5.9–5.12 and table 5.1).

The inflation figures narrow down the domestic consequences. Annual CPI inflation rose from 0.6% in May to 0.8% in August. The contribution from imports increased from 0.1 to 0.3 percentage points, while the domestic contribution held at 0.5 points. Imported petroleum products were 25.2% dearer than a year earlier in August, but other imports were still 0.9% cheaper. Rents rose 1.6%, while overall domestic services inflation eased from 1.1% to 1.0%. Two underlying measures edged higher, the federal statistical office’s core measure from 0.3% to 0.4% and the SNB’s trimmed mean from 0.5% to 0.6%. Holding the policy rate at 0%, the SNB’s forecast put inflation at 1.2% in the final quarter of 2026 and first quarter of 2027, then 0.7% in the second half of 2027. The energy assumptions mattered most near the peak. The breadth of domestic repricing mattered more for whether the rise would last (pp. 5–10, 18–21, table 1.1).

Real activity gave firms greater scope to absorb some of those costs. Second-quarter GDP rose 6.3% at a seasonally adjusted annualised rate, after adjustment for major sporting events. Exceptional chemicals and pharmaceutical output accounted for much of the increase, although other manufacturing, services and construction also grew. National accounts revisions had separately lifted the estimated level of first-quarter value added by 0.7%. The revised starting point and unusually strong quarter both helped lift the SNB’s 2026 growth projection to 1.5–2%. Its 2027 projection stayed around 1.5%. Manufacturing utilisation was still below average. Registered unemployment was 3.1% in August, while the separately defined survey-based ILO rate rose from 5.0% in the first quarter to 5.1% in the second. Neither measure supported extrapolating the pharmaceutical surge into an economy-wide shortage of workers (pp. 13–17, table 3.1 and charts 3.5–3.8).

Company interviews explain how this combination could feed through to consumer prices. Executives described rising transport and procurement costs and longer waits for some petroleum-based inputs and electronic components. Some selling prices could be reset only with a delay and some cost increases could be passed on only in part. For many firms, modest labour-cost increases mattered more than dearer intermediate goods. Average expected wage growth was 1.5% in 2026 and 1.3% in 2027, with many negotiations still ahead. Firms’ six-to-twelve-month inflation expectations actually fell from 1.2% to 1.0%, while their three-to-five-year expectation held at 1.2%. The survey gives a mechanism for the aggregate data, with a clear sampling caveat. Cyclical industries have extra weight, public administration and agriculture are excluded, and firms generally employ at least 50 people. The survey charts average qualitative scores on a five-point scale. They indicate the direction of turnover or price intentions, without supplying a percentage change in national sales or margins (pp. 28–34, especially charts 9–11).

questions.question: Did banks’ customers respond more to relative yields than to a change in credit supply?
questions.detail: Compare sight, saving and time-deposit growth with the gap between bank deposit rates and market yields. Use the same publication vintage for loans and monetary aggregates, retaining the lending classifications in table 5.1. A shift out of liquid accounts alongside sustained mortgage growth would support the allocation mechanism described by the SNB.

questions.question: How much of the franc’s depreciation can be associated with changing rate differentials?
questions.detail: Compare bilateral exchange rates with matching Swiss and foreign rates and currency volatility. Examine the periods in which uncertainty briefly strengthened the franc separately. Treat the mid-June to mid-September interval, the September decision and the later bulletin release as three different windows. Measured carry positions would provide an independent test of the proposed mechanism.

questions.question: Where did more costly inputs actually reach final selling prices?
questions.detail: Match the petroleum and other-import components with subsequent consumer prices and follow the firms most exposed to freight, packaging and electronic inputs. Compare their reported repricing intentions with realised domestic goods and services inflation. A broadening of price increases and wage settlements would change the reading of a headline acceleration initially explained by imported products.

questions.question: How much demand persisted after the pharmaceutical surge and the national accounts revisions?
questions.detail: Reconstruct the GDP profile using the vintage available at the assessment. Compare manufacturing outside pharmaceuticals, construction and services with employment, capacity utilisation and subsequent company interviews. That separates a higher historical base and a volatile quarter from sustained domestic demand relevant to pricing power and borrowing.
